Recently, media coverage has pointed to a number of lawsuits against social media companies. these lawsuits have included platforms such as meta and have included other companies such as Discord and Roblox. This insight will provide overall details on what these cases are about any as content creators what you should know about them.

## Main Point

1. MDL-3047: In Re: Social Media Adolescent Addiction/Personal Injury Products Liability Litigation
1. MDL-3166L In Re: Roblox Corporation Child Sexual Exploitation and Assualt Litigation

### What is an MDL?

MDL stands for Multi District Litigation, which is a way for the federal court system to coordiante lawsuits that share similar qualities. 

While these are two separate coordainted cases, they both are focused on platforms that are often used in content creator circles. 

#### MDL-3047 - In Re: Social Media Adolescent Addiction/Personal Injury Products Liability LItigation

Traditionally, lawsuits against social media platforms have often faced a powerful defense under [Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/47/230), usually referenced simply as Section 230. Section 230 generally prevents online platforms from being treated as the publisher or speaker of content created by third-party users. This means a platform can host user-generated content without being held legally responsible for the effects of that content.
For many years, Section 230 has blocked or limited many content-based lawsuits against social media companies. The lawsuits in MDL 3047 take a different angle. Rather than arguing only that individual posts harmed children, plaintiffs argue that the platforms’ own recommendation systems and engagement tools are part of the problem. The allegation is that social media platforms were designed to algorithmically maximize adolescent attention, repeatedly recommend engaging or harmful material, encourage compulsive use, and keep children and teens on the platform for longer periods of time.
This distinction matters because the lawsuit shifts attention from content moderation to platform architecture. The plaintiffs are effectively challenging the algorithmic systems that determine what users see, how often they see it, and how aggressively content is pushed back into their feeds. One important version of this argument is a public nuisance theory, especially in claims brought by school districts, local governments, and state attorneys general. These plaintiffs argue that engagement-driven recommendation systems have contributed to a broader youth mental-health and public-health burden, forcing public institutions to spend money on counseling, behavioral support, staff training, discipline, and other remedial services.
While my focus here is on the federal MDL, related cases are also moving through state courts. In [California](https://cand.uscourts.gov/cases-e-filing/cases/422-md-03047-ygr/re-social-media-adolescent-addictionpersonal-injury-products), a coordinated state proceeding has included bellwether trials over alleged social media addiction harms . In [New Mexico](https://nmdoj.gov/press-release/new-mexico-department-of-justice-wins-landmark-verdict-against-meta/), the Attorney General’s case against Meta has also advanced, including a consumer-protection verdict and a later public nuisance phase seeking broader remedies and platform changes.

#### MDL-3166 - In Re: Roblox Corporation Child Sexual Exploitation and Assault Litigation

MDL-3166 makes a related but somewhat different argument about child safety and platform design. Whereas MDL-3047 focuses on social media platforms allegedly using engagement-driven algorithms to keep adolescents online, MDL-3166 focuses on Roblox as a child-facing gaming and social platform that allegedly allowed predators to find, contact, groom, and exploit minors. The federal MDL, formally titled In Re: Roblox Corporation Child Sexual Exploitation and Assault Litigation, was centralized in the Northern District of California for coordinated pretrial proceedings ("JPML Transfer Order" (https://www.jpml.uscourts.gov/sites/jpml/files/MDL-3166-Transfer_Order-12-25.pdf)).

The connection to Discord is especially important for creators because Discord is often where public audiences become private communities. A YouTube channel, Twitch stream, Roblox group, or social media page may be the first point of discovery, but Discord is often where fans build closer relationships with creators, moderators, and each other. In reporting on the MDL, Reuters noted that while the lawsuits center on Roblox, many also name Meta, Snap, and Discord because conversations allegedly moved from Roblox to other communication platforms ("Reuters" (https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/child-sexual-exploitation-lawsuits-against-roblox-centralized-san-francisco-2025-12-12/)).

That does not mean creators should abandon Discord. It means creators should treat Discord servers as serious community infrastructure, not just casual fan spaces. Discord itself has built tools such as Family Center, age-restricted spaces, and sensitive-content controls that are meant to support safer teen experiences ["Discord Family Center"] (https://discord.com/safety-family-center); ["Discord Age-Restricted Channels and Content"] (https://support.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/115000084051-Age-Restricted-Channels-and-Content)). For creator communities, the practical lesson is that servers connected to a public brand should have clear rules, active moderation, limits on adult-minor private contact, reporting pathways, and careful control over channels where users can form private relationships.

The core claim in MDL-3166 is not simply that a bad actor used the internet to harm a child. The claim is that platform design choices — including weak age verification, inadequate parental controls, messaging features, social discovery tools, virtual currency, insufficient warnings, and limited moderation safeguards — created an unsafe environment for children. Put more simply, these lawsuits show how harm can move across platforms. A child may discover a community in one place, interact socially in another, and then be moved into private messages where the risk becomes harder to see.

### Key Takeaway

For creators and companies, the question is not only “What content are we posting?” but also “What kind of community system are we building around that content?”

For creators, brands, and companies that depend on social media distribution, this matters because any legal or regulatory response may not only affect platform liability. It could also affect how algorithms prioritize, recommend, suppress, or reward content. If platforms are pressured to redesign engagement systems, then creators may need to think more carefully about how their content performs under recommendation rules that may increasingly value safety, age-appropriateness, trustworthiness, and reduced compulsive-use patterns rather than pure watch time or engagement.
